title: 2 Kings 9:1–13
context: Elisha sends one of the sons of the prophets to Ramoth Gilead to anoint Jehu, an army commander, as king over Israel, fulfilling the commission first given to Elijah (1 Kings 19:16–17). In a private room the young prophet pours oil on Jehu’s head and delivers the LORD’s charge: Jehu is to strike the house of Ahab to avenge the blood of the prophets shed by Jezebel, and Ahab’s house will end like the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha. The prophet then flees. When Jehu tells his fellow officers what was said, they spread their cloaks beneath him, sound the trumpet, and proclaim him king.

verses.text: Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets, and said to him, “Put your belt on your waist, take this vial of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha sends a young prophet with oil to Ramoth Gilead. Arminian readers note that God works through human messengers and prophets, giving them real tasks to carry out in obedience to his word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the commission given to Elijah in 1 Kings 19:16 now carried out through Elisha, showing that God’s purposes reach their appointed time. Shared ground: the anointing is presented as a prophetic act directed by the LORD.

verses.text: When you come there, find Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi, and go in and make him rise up from among his brothers, and take him to an inner room.
verses.arminianNotes: The young prophet is to find Jehu, take him aside, and bring him into an inner room. Arminian readers note the secrecy, which protects the messenger and gives Jehu the chance to receive the word privately.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the private setting as underscoring that the kingship comes from God’s word, not from public acclaim. Both traditions read the instructions as practical, while noting that Ramoth Gilead was a frontier town whose exact site is debated.

verses.text: Then take the vial of oil, and pour it on his head, and say, ‘The LORD says, “I have anointed you king over Israel.” ’ Then open the door, flee, and don’t wait.”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet is to anoint Jehu, declare the LORD’s word, then flee without waiting. Arminian readers see urgency and danger in the instructions, since anointing a rival king was an act of great political risk.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the brief, decisive act as showing that God’s word accomplishes its purpose without lengthy explanation. Shared ground: the prophet’s role is to deliver the message faithfully and leave the outcome in God’s hands.

verses.text: So the young man, the young prophet, went to Ramoth Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: The young prophet goes to Ramoth Gilead. Arminian readers note his prompt obedience, a small but real act of faithfulness that sets in motion a major turn in Israel’s history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the unnamed messenger as an example of how God uses humble servants to carry out his purposes. Both traditions read the short verse as showing obedience to the prophetic word without hesitation.

verses.text: When he came, behold, the captains of the army were sitting. Then he said, “I have a message for you, captain.” Jehu said, “To which one of us?” He said, “To you, O captain.”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet finds the captains sitting together and says he has a word for one of them. Arminian readers note the tension of the moment, as Jehu must step forward among his peers to receive the message.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God singling out Jehu from among the commanders, as the prophet confirms which captain is meant. Shared ground: the scene highlights that the choice of Jehu is specific and comes through the prophet’s word.

verses.text: He arose, and went into the house. Then he poured the oil on his head, and said to him, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘I have anointed you king over the people of the LORD, even over Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet pours oil on Jehu and declares that the LORD has anointed him king over the LORD’s people. Arminian readers note the phrase “the people of the LORD,” which reminds Jehu whose people he will rule.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jehu’s authority as derived from God’s appointment. Both traditions read the anointing as a real commission, while the narrative will later evaluate how faithfully Jehu carries it out (10:29–31).

verses.text: You must strike your master Ahab’s house, that I may avenge the blood of my servants the prophets, and the blood of all the servants of the LORD, at the hand of Jezebel.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu is to strike Ahab’s house to avenge the blood of the prophets shed by Jezebel. Arminian readers note that the charge is tied to specific crimes, including the killing of the LORD’s prophets (1 Kings 18:4, 13).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s justice for the blood of his servants, delayed but not forgotten. Shared ground: both traditions read the command as judgment on the guilty dynasty for its violence against the LORD’s servants, not as a general warrant.

verses.text: For the whole house of Ahab will perish. I will cut off from Ahab everyone who urinates against a wall, both him who is shut up and him who is left at large in Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The whole house of Ahab will perish, every male cut off. Arminian readers note that the language repeats the prophetic sentence given to Ahab earlier (1 Kings 21:21), showing judgment announced long before it falls.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sentence as God’s word on a dynasty that had led Israel deeply into idolatry. Both traditions report the severity of the language soberly, reading it as specific to Ahab’s house and its history.

verses.text: I will make Ahab’s house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab’s house will become like the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha. Arminian readers note the pattern of dynasties that fell under judgment for leading Israel into sin (1 Kings 14:10–11; 16:3–4).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the comparison as showing that God’s judgment on persistent rebellion follows a consistent pattern. Shared ground: the verse places Ahab’s house within a history of royal houses judged for their sins.

verses.text: The dogs will eat Jezebel on the plot of ground of Jezreel, and there shall be no one to bury her.’ ” Then he opened the door and fled.
verses.arminianNotes: Dogs will eat Jezebel in Jezreel, and no one will bury her; then the prophet flees. Arminian readers note that the word against Jezebel repeats Elijah’s earlier prophecy (1 Kings 21:23), linking her end to her own deeds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophecy as establishing in advance the meaning of what will happen to her. Both traditions read the word as judgment announced by God, which the narrative will report soberly when it is fulfilled in 9:35–37.

verses.text: When Jehu came out to the servants of his lord and one said to him, “Is all well? Why did this madman come to you?” He said to them, “You know the man and how he talks.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu’s fellow officers ask why “this madman” came, and Jehu at first deflects. Arminian readers note that prophets were sometimes regarded with suspicion or contempt, even by those who knew their message mattered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the officers’ dismissive language as revealing the low regard for the LORD’s prophets in Israel at this time. Shared ground: Jehu’s evasion shows caution before he reveals the anointing to his peers.

verses.text: They said, “That is a lie. Tell us now.” He said, “He said to me, ‘The LORD says, I have anointed you king over Israel.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The officers insist, and Jehu tells them the LORD has anointed him king. Arminian readers note that Jehu shares the word openly once pressed, putting the decision to his fellow officers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the word of the LORD spreading despite Jehu’s initial reluctance to speak it. Both traditions read the verse as the turning point when the private anointing becomes known among the leaders of the army.

verses.text: Then they hurried, and each man took his cloak, and put it under him on the top of the stairs, and blew the trumpet, saying, “Jehu is king.”
verses.arminianNotes: The officers spread their cloaks under Jehu, sound the trumpet, and proclaim him king. Arminian readers see a quick and willing response, as the army leaders accept Jehu’s kingship without delay.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the public acclamation as following the prophetic anointing, with God’s choice now recognized by the people. Shared ground: the scene marks the beginning of Jehu’s reign and the start of the coup against Joram.
